data.title: Hungarians and Slovaks share breakfast on Danube bridge that survived war and division
data.description:
Hungarians and Slovaks share breakfast on Danube bridge that survived war and division

By Krisztina Fenyo
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 11:07 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Hungarians and Slovaks share breakfast on Danube bridge to build ties

1 of 6
Hungarians and Slovaks talk during a shared breakfast on the Maria Valeria bridge between Esztergom, Hungary, and Sturovo, Slovakia, during an event to foster ties between communities with a history of ethnic tensions, in Esztergom, Hungary, September 19, 2026. REUTERS/Marton Monus

By Krisztina Fenyo

ESZTERGOM, Hungary/STUROVO, Slovakia, Sept 19 (Reuters) - A historic bridge linking Hungary and Slovakia became an unlikely breakfast venue on ‌Saturday, as locals gathered on the Danube crossing to celebrate friendship ‌between the two neighbouring communities.

The Maria Valeria Bridge, which connects Esztergom in Hungary and Sturovo ​in Slovakia, has twice been destroyed and rebuilt since it first opened in 1895.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In late 1944, as World War Two drew to a close, retreating German troops blew up its three middle sections. The bridge then lay ‌neglected for nearly 60 years, ⁠forcing people to cross the border by ferry during decades of communist rule. It reopened in its original glory ⁠in 2001.

On Saturday, dozens of tables were laid out along the bridge for a community breakfast of croissants, ham, cheese and coffee. Participants from both towns ​were ​paired based on their interests and languages, ​encouraging new cross-border friendships.

"I think ‌the people of Esztergom and Parkany could mix a bit more," organiser Norbert Nagy said.

Ethnic Hungarians make up about 9% of Slovakia's 5.5 million people, and many live in Sturovo, known in Hungarian as Parkany.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I met a really lovely and kind person here this morning on the bridge, so ‌it was a great experience for me," ​said Mark Zelenak, who arrived from Esztergom.

Hungary ​and Slovakia have shared open ​borders since both joined Europe's Schengen zone in 2007, ‌although political tensions have occasionally surfaced ​over Slovakia's ethnic Hungarian ​minority.

But Laszlo Valacsay, who also took part in the breakfast, said such tensions were often stirred by politicians, while local people lived ​peacefully side by side.

"It ‌was always generated, but not by the people, by us, ​who live here..no, no," he said.

(Reporting by Krisztina Fenyo, writing by ​Krisztina Than; Editing by Ros Russell)

data.title: Saudi capital issues first air raid alert since renewed fighting in Yemen
data.description:
Saudi capital issues first air raid alert since renewed fighting in Yemen

AFP News
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 11:03 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Saudi authorities issued their first air raid alert in the capital since fighting returned to neighbouring Yemen, leaving residents of Riyadh rattled after they heard explosions ringing out in the early hours of Saturday.

Yemen's Houthis have staged a lightning offensive this month, seizing swathes of territory in one of the world's poorest countries, leaving the internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, scrambling to respond.

Saudi Arabia itself, one of the region's powerhouses, has conducted scores of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas but failed to stop the advance. It has also sought help from its ally, the United States, but that has not materialised.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

This is the first time since Yemen's long-standing civil war resumed that it has threatened the Saudi capital, further shaking a global economy already under pressure by nearly seven months of war between the US and Iran.

"The area is under a hostile aerial threat," said a message received just before 3:00 am by Riyadh residents, urging them to stay indoors.

AFP journalists then heard two explosions, before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later.

"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," a Riyadh resident, 27, living in the city's north, told AFP.

"It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- 'Terrifying' -

Another resident described the attack as "terrifying".

"I was extremely anxious -- especially because, unlike previous times, the 'all-clear' signal didn't come right away," the central Riyadh resident said.

Saudi Arabia has not commented on the threat mentioned in the warnings sent overnight to residents of several regions and has not identified where it originated from.

The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Wednesday, denouncing it as a "cowardly terrorist attack" on Islam's holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year, both Sunnis and Shias.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Iran-backed Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a "worn-out lie".

The group has reported scores of retaliatory strikes carried out daily by Riyadh since their lightning offensive this month to take over the country's entire Red Sea coast, giving them control over the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.

Riyadh was targeted with waves of attacks during an earlier iteration of the war, including a drone strike on the US embassy in the capital's diplomatic quarter in March.

The United States, according to Axios, last week refused to strike the Houthis at Saudi Arabia's request.

On Thursday, Washington approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom to help Riyadh "deter current and future threats", the US State Department said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- Reduced Saudi exports -

The United Nations said on Friday that the renewed fighting had displaced more than 112,000 people while nearly 3,000 others had fled across the sea to Djibouti.

The war in Yemen broke out in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the capital Sanaa and other regions, triggering a military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in March 2015.

The fragile truce reached in 2022 between the warring parties collapsed in July, when the Houthis defied Riyadh's control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in Yemen.

Their recent takeover of the coastline has sparked global concern, with international maritime trade already heavily impacted by Iran's imposition of a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz since the Middle East war erupted in late February.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Houthis insist there is no threat to shipping in the sea lane -- except for Saudi ships, from the world's leading crude exporter.

The attack targeting Riyadh comes as the Houthis improve their defences in newly conquered territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline, with members of the group telling AFP they have been installing radar and digging tunnels.

Two separate Houthi sources told AFP that Iranian Revolutionary Guards had visited the area in recent days.

Figures from maritime tracking firm Kpler showed that Saudi exports via the Bab al-Mandab strait had dropped since July, although five loaded ships had passed through in the last week.

data.title: Trump’s Aggressive Reaction To A Female Journalist Just Taught Us All A New Term
data.description:
Trump’s Aggressive Reaction To A Female Journalist Just Taught Us All A New Term

Caroline Bologna
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 11:00 am UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump has a tendency to go after female reporters. Last Thursday night, he turned his sights on ABC's Rachel Scott, and body language experts say what happened next was a textbook intimidation display.

Scott pressed Trump about his preposterous promise to send $5,000 checks to every adult citizen in the U.S. if Republicans win the midterm elections.

Life: People Are Celebrating Joyce Beatty For Standing Up To Trump — Here's What She Said That's So Huge

"If your economic policies are working, why do you need an incentive for people to turn out to vote?" she asked.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Avoiding the question, the president responded, "I didn't do it for turning out the vote. I did it as a reward for people having to put up with five years and four years of horrible, a horrible situation caused by Biden," he said, later adding. "It's almost a reward for the people having to put up with Biden's policies."

When Scott tried to ask a follow-up question about the tariff refund checks Trump had previously promised, he cut her off with "Not you! Not you!" Then, he moved in closer to her face and took on a growling tone as he said, "Hey! Not you!"

"Your network and you, you're the worst," he added.

Politics: 'Not You!': Trump Flips Out On Female Reporter After A Very Basic Question

Traci Brown, a body language expert and behavior analyst, was struck by the physical dimension of Trump's response, particularly the moment he leaned toward Scott.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He is getting on her level, eye to eye, in her face, to threaten and scare her a bit," she told HuffPost.

Rather than let the reporter ask her follow-up question and continue to engage in a back-and-forth dialogue, Trump was "trying to wrestle back control," said clinical psychologist and behavioral expert Denise Dudley.

She identified the president's response as a specific behavioral technique: proxemic intrusion. Basically, it refers to a deliberate violation of personal space used to assert dominance and signal aggression

Life: Aw, Kash Patel Thinks He Can Pull Off This Trump Trademark

"Proxemic intrusion is an aggressive move, and it's kind of scary to us," Dudley explained. "Human beings and mammals in general are very sensitive to proxemic intrusion because evolutionarily and biologically, we see that as somebody coming in at us and we don't know if they're friend or foe."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Body language and nonverbal communication expert Patti Wood tracked the escalation in Trump's physical behavior, particularly as he moved closer to Scott when she tried to ask a follow-up question.

"His voice rose. He angrily yells at her, 'Hey, not you' the first time, and he steps closer and leans in and repeats with his mouth and lips overworking, overarticulating," she said. "He gives a focused glare of anger with lowered, drawn-together eyebrows."

Then it escalated further. "He moves in closer, leaning in with his full upper body and head closer to her personal zone of space, less than two feet," Wood said. "We see his jaw and chin tighten and his lips thin and tighten. The lips narrowing is a very reliable sign of anger."

Life: Trump's Latest 'Unhinged' Attack On A Female Journalist Is 'Quite Alarming,' Experts Say

She noted that Trump's anger was not controlled, as his thin lips jutted outward rather than staying closed to contain the emotion.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He singles her out and goes into full attack mode, getting up in her face. His relentless glare of dominance becomes more focused as he attacks, mouth open, upper lip thinning and raised, and teeth showing in a symbolic biting motion as he yells viciously for the third time, 'NOT YOU.'"

Wood also flagged something significant about the duration of the outburst itself.

"Most emotional expressions last very briefly ― two seconds or less in adults, then the adult controls their emotions," she said. "This extended emotional outburst of anger shows his lack of emotional control, which also makes it more frightening."

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Dudley also viewed the move as part of a broader strategy.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He's using what we would call multimodal intensification ― a technique where he uses everything at once," she said. "His voice gets louder, and at one point there's a kind of guttural sound that comes in. His movement changes with proxemic intrusion. His gaze gets really intense. And he's pointing, so making a gesture."

Life: Experts Spot An Extreme Flaw In Katie Miller's Pro-Flock Camera Rationale

On the pointing specifically, Dudley was emphatic.

"Unless you're literally pointing the direction to the bathroom down the hall, you just don't ever point," she said. "Pointing is aggressive. Even though it's your finger, you're pointing a sharp object at somebody, and human beings are sensitive to that."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

These physical changes align with his language and the intensity of his "you're the worst" insult.

"He's definitely exhibiting cluster congruence, or channel congruence," Dudley said. "All the behavioral clusters or channels are saying the same thing. There's no mixed message here. The cluster is congruent. It's verbal and nonverbal signals communicating the same message, which is: I'm done with you, I don't like you, I'm not going to let you keep the floor, and I'm going to go at you."

On the whole, she also sees a menacing vibe to the behavior as well.

"He's pointing and moving in, and the way his face contorts when he leans in, it's threatening," Dudley said. "If somebody leaned in at you and made that face and pointed at you and used that voice tone, you would probably back up. That's what I would do."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Scott did not appear to back up, and both experts found that revealing as well.

"He warned her, waved her off, dismissing her, and she keeps going," Brown said. "That's what reporters do, so there's nothing unusual with her behavior. What is unusual is the stimulus doesn't match the response."

Wood noted the particular vulnerability of Scott's position.

"The attack is full-on and frightening, and what makes it even more frightening is that her position as a journalist and the question she asked were reasonable," she observed. "Just as he has done to other female reporters, he isolates her from the other reporters. She is a female enduring a vicious public attack that she can't defend against or retreat from and keep her job, and no one else comes to defend or protect her. Also, notice she does not sound frightened."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Although Trump has been hostile toward male journalists as well, his attacksonwomenreporters have been particularly brutal ― including calling The New York Times' Katie Rogers "ugly," dismissing CNN's Kaitlan Collins as "very dumb and unhappy," dubbing Maggie Haberman "Maggot Hagerman," telling Bloomberg's Catherine Lucey "Quiet, piggy!" and attacking ABC's Mary Bruce for asking what he called "a horrible, insubordinate, and just a terrible question."

Dudley described Scott's composure in this latest exchange with the president as bravery and professionalism in the face of "aggressive, threatening" behavior.

"This is a good moment for her as a reporter," she said. "The natural response of somebody getting in your face and pointing at you and using that voice tone would be to back up because we as humans sense we're in physical danger. But I would assume that natural response in her is suppressed because her energy and her adrenaline is around getting the story, trying to maintain the floor. And he's trying to get that conversational control away from her."

Additionally, Dudley observed that the president's anger and eruption seemed clearly targeted, rather than general.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It's not like he's just generally agitated or in a bad mood and mad at all reporters," she said. "When he turns to the next reporter, it's like 'OK, what is your question?' His aggression is aimed right at her. Or he'd be mad at the other guy, but he's clearly not."

The original version of this story was published on HuffPost at an earlier date.

data.title: People Are Celebrating Joyce Beatty For Standing Up To Trump — Here’s What She Said That’s So Huge
data.description:
People Are Celebrating Joyce Beatty For Standing Up To Trump — Here’s What She Said That’s So Huge

Katie Mather
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 11:00 am UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) sparked strong internet reactions when on Tuesday she recounted a heated exchange she had with President Donald Trump.

While on MS Now's "The Weeknight," Beatty described the moment Trump lost the legal battle to put his name on the Kennedy Center.

Life: Body Language Experts Have A LOT To Say About Elizabeth Holmes' Facial Expressions In New Documentary

"Let me just make it simple: It was the most unprofessional thing that I have ever witnessed or been a part of," Beatty said. "He went into name-calling, from everything from trying to say that I was an obstructionist, I was dumb."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"He said, 'I think you're incompetent.' And I said, 'I know you're incompetent,'" Beatty continued. "I was not going to let him call me awful things."

Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's board of trustees since 2019, attended Tuesday morning's virtual board meeting, where the board voted to close the center, citing its "dire" financial and structural shape.

The vote came about half an hour after a federal judge rejected the board's latest attempt to add Trump's name to the building, which the Trump administration has already appealed. Trump has repeatedly said he will shut down all renovations unless his name is attached to the memorial for late President John F. Kennedy. In a Truth Social post Tuesday night, Trump claimed that he funneled $17 million into the Kennedy Center "to keep it afloat."

"He said he was going to hold me responsible if something fell out of the ceiling and killed someone, and I told him, I said, 'You're already killing people. We're at war. We also have people who are starving. You're doing this," Beatty said. "And then he wanted to talk about how great he was with developing, and he didn't know anything about me, but I had never done anything. This was the biggest thing I had done. So I reminded him that he had more bankruptcies than anybody in the room."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

In a separate interview with CNN, Beatty told host Kaitlan Collins that she believed Trump "made it personal" against her because her name is on the lawsuit to stop him from renaming the Kennedy Center.

"I think it would be unthinkable for someone to hear a president using the language he used," Beatty told Collins. "He threw a tantrum. It was like an immature child. I wouldn't even want to put this on a child. It was just being very — in my opinion — very immature, shouting, calling names."

Life: People Are Celebrating Joyce Beatty For Standing Up To Trump — Here's What She Said That's So Huge

Beatty has publicly challenged Trump's attempts to get his name on the Kennedy Center, and said in a statement issued on Tuesday that the president is "holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial." Beatty's team did not respond to HuffPost's request for comment.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"For decades, Democrats let the Kennedy Center rot as water damage spread, infrastructure crumbled, and a national treasure fell apart under their watch," White House spokesperson Liz Huston told HuffPost. "President Trump did what Democrats wouldn't by finally committing the resources and the leadership needed to restore the Kennedy Center and make it the finest performing arts facility in the world."

Personal attacks in professional settings "isn't new," particularly against women of color, Nadia Brown, a professor of government and chair of the women's and gender studies program at Georgetown University, told HuffPost.

"What makes this different here is that, although she's a congresswoman [and] Trump is the president, they're in a different context: They're serving on a board together," Brown said. "The power hierarchy exists, but not in the same way as it exists when he's the president of the United States, and she's one of 435 members of the U.S. House."

Politics: Court Says Trump Can't Name The Kennedy Center After Himself

Brown said Trump's outburst struck her as even more surprising in this context. Board members, she said, are expected to work toward a shared goal, and when they don't, the fallout is usually private.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"If there are people that have blowups … they typically go away or they [get] put off the board or decide not to run again, but not in this public fashion," Brown said. "This is pretty eye-opening here."

Brown said the reaction to Beatty's story isn't universal, though. It's landing the hardest with people who were "eager for Democrats to push back" and knew Beatty's lines (such as "you have more bankruptcies than anyone in the room") were true. People less familiar with the Kennedy Center dispute, she said, "might have other thoughts about this," while those already "waiting for Democrats to respond" and are aware of the dynamics at play "are able to move past" any reflexive judgment of Beatty's tone.

This reflexive judgment, Brown said, is what Beatty may have been navigating by going on MS Now and CNN later that night to tell her story herself.

Life: Experts Spot An Extreme Flaw In Katie Miller's Pro-Flock Camera Rationale

Brown traced the trope of angry Black women back to slavery, with Michelle Wallace's 1979 book putting the phenomenon into explicit terms. Sociologist Patricia Hill Collins later explained why the trope still endures, Brown said, because anger expressed by Black women is rarely read as "justified or righteous emotion" — which can make it easy to dismiss.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"This is from Black women [in] Congress to the Black woman that is working at the grocery store," Brown said. "Black women writ large have this stereotype."

Brown said Beatty's decision to discuss the exchange publicly, including with MS Now and CNN, may reflect an awareness of this risk and an attempt to frame the moment on Beatty's terms, "getting ahead of … the Trump machine."

The original version of this story was published on HuffPost at an earlier date.

data.title: After deaths of nine women, South Africans gather to run, mourn and demand change
data.description:
After deaths of nine women, South Africans gather to run, mourn and demand change

Reuters
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 10:48 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A vigil for victims of gender-based violence and femicide, in Cape Town

1 of 3
A student holds a placard at the University of Cape Town during a vigil for victims of gender-based violence and femicide, while calling for stronger action against violence against women following a spate of killings in recent months around Johannesburg, in Cape Town, South Africa, September 18, 2026. REUTERS/Esa Alexander

JOHANNESBURG, Sept 19 (Reuters) - South Africans gathered for memorial runs and protests this week after the killings of nine women near Johannesburg reignited anger and fear over violence that ‌many say mirrors the dangers women face every day.

Police have found the bodies of nine ‌women in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months and are investigating whether the killings are linked.

Most of the victims ​were in their 20s and 30s. Some were found stripped of their clothes and showed signs of sexual assault.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A memorial run in Johannesburg on Saturday morning honoured one of the victims, Elizabeth Moselakgomo, who disappeared after going for a run and was found dead days later. Runners lit candles and carried a banner reading: "Enough. ‌Stop Femicide."

"We are here because we've ⁠lost a runner. But we are not safe anywhere," said Lerato Lentsela, one of dozens of people who dressed in black for the memorial run.

"We are not ⁠safe running, we are not safe at a post office, we are not safe on a date, we are not safe in our own homes, we are not safe in an Uber."

The killings have reignited anger over violence ​against ​women in South Africa, where gender-based violence was declared ​a national disaster in 2025. Many women say ‌the heightened attention and official promises have done little to make them feel safer.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Enough is enough. Our women deserve to live, walk, run and exist without fear," the Uyinene Mrwetyana Foundation, a charity that campaigns against gender-based violence, said in a statement.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Thursday that South Africa could not allow itself to grow accustomed to such violence and pledged that no stone would be left unturned ‌in the investigations.

But policing in South Africa is weakened by ​corruption and lack of resources. Only about one in 10 ​murders is ever solved.

"We need to relook at ​our policing. The only reason these nine women were found was because there ‌was more police presence in the area. This ​problem is countrywide," said ​Merlize Jogiat of Women for Change, which held a memorial event in Cape Town on Friday.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Some women also criticised police advice urging them to take extra precautions when exercising or walking alone.

"Stop ​placing the responsibility of our safety ‌back onto us," Women for Change said in a social media post. "Women should not have ​to organise their entire lives around surviving violence and not being next."

(Reporting by Nellie ​Peyton and Thando Hlope;Editing by Bate Felix, Aidan Lewis)

data.title: Frustration grows as Houthis widen Middle East conflict with US unwilling to intervene
data.description:
Frustration grows as Houthis widen Middle East conflict with US unwilling to intervene

Kylie Atwood, Jennifer Hansler, Zachary Cohen, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 10:16 am UTC
9 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Dramatic recent advances by the Iran-backed Houthis, including the seizure of a strategically important island in the Red Sea, have dealt another blow to a region reeling from the US war with Iran and exacerbated an already severe global energy crisis. But neither the US nor its key ally Saudi Arabia has a clear plan to beat back the group, multiple sources told CNN, leading many in the region to ask where the counteroffensive will come from.

Although US officials acknowledge the Yemeni rebel group is advancing with the goal of ultimately asserting control over the critical Bab al Mandeb Strait, the Trump administration is signaling it has little interest in using the American military to stop them – relying instead on Saudi Arabia to do so.

But even with additional US intelligence and targeting support, Saudi Arabia has not been able to effectively stop the Houthis from taking key coastal towns in Yemen, frustrating Gulf and American officials. Sources who spoke with CNN expressed doubt that the Saudis would be able to stop the Houthis on their own.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Houthis moves have not come as a surprise to sources in the region, as well as former diplomats, who said the weaknesses of the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces were well-known. For months US intelligence reports indicated the group would attempt to close another key waterway for commercial shipping as Iran did earlier this year, US officials said.

Still, the US believes it is currently providing Saudi Arabia with everything it needs to be successful against the Houthis, one American official told CNN, referring to the recent increase in sharing intelligence support and sharing of targeting data support with the Kingdom. And after about a decade of training the Yemen government's military, the Kingdom had assured US officials that they were confident in their ability, two sources told CNN.

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces started fighting the Houthis, who are supported and trained by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), more than a decade ago during Yemen's brutal civil war. A 2022 UN-brokered truce had brought a period of relatively low levels of hostilities between the two sides.

However, the fighting has resumed and intensified in recent weeks. The Saudis accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca, Islam's holiest city, and the Houthis claim to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet. In the past day alerts sounded for the first time in the capital Riyadh.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

President Donald Trump has made clear that his current red line is direct US participation in kinetic strikes against the Houthis. To date, US military support has been strictly providing intel and targeting data for Saudi strikes.

"No offensive strikes," said a US official.

'The Houthis called us and they don't want to fight'

Multiple Gulf and US sources say messaging from Trump signals to the Iranians he is unwilling to back US allies in the region.

"The Houthis called us and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said in remarks to reporters in Ireland last weekend. "They don't want us to go after them and would much prefer not having us involved and they're letting most ships go through."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It's just one country they're not too happy with," Trump said, referring to Saudi Arabia, "and we'll get that straightened out."

Barbara Leaf, a former US diplomat who worked throughout the Middle East called Trump's own comments about the Houthis "shocking."

"It's a pretty harsh way to treat your relationship with a close partner, to appear to privilege your agreement with a group you've designated as an (foreign terrorist organization) that attacked that partner," she told CNN. The administration designated the Houthis as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in March 2025.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice with Trump last week to ask for US strikes against the Houthis. That request, so far, has been rebuffed and sources said it is hard to tell if the administration policy will shift.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Amid this frustration over the Houthis advances, many Gulf sources believe the offensive represents a new front in the Iran war that could prolong the conflict. Despite some efforts to deal with the issues separately, sources increasingly believe there is unlikely to be progress on Iran without dealing with the Houthis.

"The Houthis' Red Sea push is emboldening the IRGC. The Saudis have to get this fixed, otherwise they are negotiating with a gun on the table and they won't do that," said Joey Hood, a former US ambassador who spent much of his career working in the Middle East.

Hood, like other sources, noted that although the Houthis claim their fight is just with Saudis, there is a clear nexus to Iran.

"Iran is in an existential battle now and pulling on all of their proxies to fight. The Houthis are not remote-controlled by Iran but they need fuel from them. So, the Houthi statements of why they are carrying out this offensive now are not a complete reflection of reality," said Hood.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The situation in Yemen has complicated the other negotiations, including those over the Strait of Hormuz.

A first meeting between Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and Iran since the US-Iran war began was canceled earlier this week. Saudi Arabia decided not to attend amid concerns around the language of a potential agreement between Oman and Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz and other Gulf countries followed suit. Regional sources said it was a clear signal that the Kingdom sees no upside to engaging with the Iranians amid active Houthi attacks.

"Due to the Houthi attacks and the situation near the Bab-el-Mandeb corridor, it's affecting the Strait of Hormuz deal," a regional source told CNN. "The Saudis are demanding an all-or-nothing approach, which is understandable, but it delays the process."

'No one wants to fight alone'

For about a decade, the Saudis have been training Yemen's military, and so far, those forces have been unable to effectively push back the Houthis. Saudi strikes, backed by US intelligence and precision targeting, have prevented the militia from exercising a firm command over some of the territory they have taken, but advances have not been wholly rebuffed.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The highest levels of the US government largely ignored the Houthi threat over the last decade despite lower-level US officials and regional players urging closer attention to the rebel group as it grew stronger, sources said. Last year's US military campaign against the Houthis also laid bare the limits of American firepower – as months of bombing failed to effectively dislodge the group's foothold inside Yemen and ended with an abrupt US-Houthi ceasefire.

The US "solidified the ceasefire" with the Houthis during a meeting in Oman this weekend, the US official said – a message that underscores the administration's unwillingness to get involved.

"The Americans sent a message," a senior Houthi official familiar with the matter told CNN Thursday, "that they don't want to join the Saudis and be part of the conflict."

"We received this message positively," the source added.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

There was a perception that Saudi Arabia's own firepower coupled with its investment in Yemen's military could counterbalance the Houthis' offenses, some current and former US officials say. That expectation has not panned out.

Others say the Houthi successes are hardly surprising, especially given unity of the militia and Iran's support.

"The Houthis have the advantage of having this really deep and productive relationship with the (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) which has trained them and taken them up several notches from the hard-scrabble kind of cave fighters that they were 12 years ago to a force that can really be quite devastating," said Leaf, who was a former Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs.

"The Houthi have spent a lot of time in the last months preparing their forces for just this kind of move," she continued. "They punched through the Saudi-aligned and Yemeni government-aligned forces, not surprisingly, just punched through them – the forces just disintegrated."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"No one wants to fight alone," said a current Gulf official. "Either the Saudis fight or they cut a deal with the Houthis."

But as it becomes clear that the Saudi-backed government will need more resources to take on the Houthis, the kingdom is also spread thin as they manage a wide array of challenges resulting from the ongoing war: a recent strike on their East-West pipeline, working with the US military on enabling tanker traffic through the strait, and keeping open a land-bridge to move critical resources through the region.

Saudi Arabia also cut oil exports to Europe for the month of September in recent days, triggering a recognition that the global energy crisis could deepen.

An effective pushback at the hands of Saudi-backed forces in Yemen is likely to require additional boots on the ground from Saudi Arabia or elsewhere, and a projection of commitment from the US, sources said. But neither of those inputs seem likely.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"At least the possibility of US involvement needs to hang over everyone to act as a deterrent, if you just unnecessarily wipe that away its demoralizing particularly to the Yemenis on the ground," another regional source said.

Leaf said she has not heard exasperation with the Saudis from officials in the region, but rather questions of "What the hell is the US going to do here?"

Gulf and US sources have also expressed doubts about whether the Houthi escalation can actually be entirely resolved militarily.

"They have been trying for years" to defeat the Houthis, the regional source said, noting that military action "will weaken them, yes, but will not end them."

CNN's Nadeen Ebrahim contributed reporting.

data.title: Greenland, Denmark say US deal will not cede sovereignty
data.description:
Greenland, Denmark say US deal will not cede sovereignty

By Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 10:09 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

FILE PHOTO: Denmark's Minister of Defense visits NATO military exercise Arctic Shield 2026

1 of 2
FILE PHOTO: Denmark's Minister of Defense Jeppe Bruus, along with Greenland's Minister for Foreign Affairs Mute B. Egede, visits the NATO military exercise Arctic Shield 2026 in Narsarsuaq, Greenland, on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Ritzau Scanpix/Mads Claus Rasmussenvia REUTERS

By Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen

COPENHAGEN, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would ‌give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic island's security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The United States, Denmark and Greenland ‌said late on Friday they had entered into an agreement for the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US ​adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of US military presence in the self-governed Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next ‌week, would end months of uncertainty triggered ⁠by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland.

"Next week could be a good week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a statement posted ⁠on Facebook on Saturday.

"A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe - while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom's red lines," he said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Denmark and Greenland ​have ​repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom ​and accept that Greenland is not for sale.

Trump ‌said on Truth Social late on Friday that under a deal, "the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America."

The deal "gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without ‌Washington's express written approval.

Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that ​the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I am pleased ​on Greenland's behalf that we are nearing the ​conclusion of an agreement - an agreement that benefits not only our collective security but also the ‌continued development of this country," Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen ​said on Saturday in a ​post on Facebook.

"The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination," he added.

Trump's threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within ​NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into ‌negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which ​would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region."

(Reporting by Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen, Additional ​reporting by Lili Bayer in Brussels; Editing by Ros Russell)

CHISINAU, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Russia's parliamentary election has triggered a diplomatic row with Moldova over its objections to the Kremlin's ‌plan to open 15 polling stations for Russian nationals in ‌the separatist Transdniestria Region.

Moscow says 220,000 residents of pro-Russian Transdniestria, a sliver of land ​which broke away from Moldova in 1990 at the end of Soviet rule, hold Russian passports and are entitled to vote on Sunday in the election for the State Duma.

Moldova's pro-Western government, which wants to join ‌the European Union by ⁠2030 and denounces the Kremlin's war in Ukraine, says Russians may vote only in a single polling station ⁠in the Russian embassy in the capital Chisinau.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It contests the 220,000 figure and opposes any polling station in Transdniestria, where it has no control ​over procedures.

Moldovan ​authorities this week denounced the Kremlin's ​15 planned polling stations as "unacceptable ‌and hostile" and summoned Russian ambassador Oleg Ozerov to the Foreign Ministry.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova retorted by urging Moldova to drop its objections and halt actions that "run against democracy, international law and common sense".

Moldovan Foreign Minister Mihail Popsoi told Moscow "not to interfere with Moldova's ‌plans for peaceful reintegration" of the ​breakaway territory.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In Russia's last parliamentary election in ​2021, authorities in Moscow opened ​27 polling stations in the region and more than ‌59,000 voters cast ballots - with ​76.2% backing the United ​Russia party which supports Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Transdniestria is not internationally recognised, not even by Moscow, though a Russian military contingent of ​some 1,500 troops, ‌which Russia sometimes describes as peacekeepers, remains stationed there despite ​demands from Moldova for them to leave.

(Reporting by Alexander Tanas, ​writing by Ron Popeski, Kirsten Donovan)

data.title: Democrats try to ride data center backlash to election victory in rural US Midwest
data.description:
Democrats try to ride data center backlash to election victory in rural US Midwest

By Valerie Volcovici
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 10:05 am UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Valerie Volcovici

Sept 19 (Reuters) - No company has announced plans for a data center in Defiance, a city of 17,000 people surrounded by soybean fields in northwestern Ohio.

But people in the aptly named community are not taking any chances.

After learning the county's economic development group had fielded inquiries from tech companies, residents spent months gathering signatures for a November 3 ballot measure to ban all but the smallest ‌data centers. City officials announced a six-month moratorium on new project approvals.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The fight in Defiance is part of a broader political backlash throughout Ohio — and across the nation — where mounting public anxiety about AI and cloud-computing infrastructure ‌has transformed data center construction from an economic success story into a contentious midterm elections issue.

Many in Defiance were already concerned about the impacts of AI development on farmland, electricity demand and water consumption. Their misgivings deepened this summer after the release of state tax records showing Ohio had foregone ​more than $2 billion in sales-tax revenue through data-center incentives in 2024 and 2025, benefiting companies such as Amazon and Meta.

Some 71% of Ohioans would now support a temporary ban on new data center construction, according to an August 31 poll from Bowling Green State University.

"Most people feel preyed upon by big business," said Becca Rupp, founder of Citizens for Responsible Development - efiance.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The groundswell building against data centers during election season has given Democratic candidates a new opening in the rural US Midwest, where they have struggled to compete during Donald Trump's presidency. Ohio is one of a handful of states with competitive races expected to decide control of Congress.

Ohio's Republican Governor Mike DeWine has suspended new applications for data center tax exemptions pending legislative reforms, but state lawmakers did not act before summer ‌recess, leaving the future of AI development in Ohio uncertain — and ripe for political ⁠attack.

CLASH OVER TAX INCENTIVES

Democratic US Representative Marcy Kaptur faces one of the toughest reelection races of her four-decade congressional career, in a newly redrawn district that includes Defiance and other conservative rural areas.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

She has leaned heavily into data-center messaging, running television ads accusing her Republican opponent Derek Merrin of supporting the unpopular tax incentives.

In a statement, Kaptur linked data centers to rising utility costs and ⁠wider concerns about corporate influence.

"Politicians are letting these companies pass the costs of their enormous energy and utility demands onto Ohio ratepayers, then handing them billions in tax breaks to sweeten the deal," she said. Residential electricity bills in Defiance rose 10% to 15% in June from a year earlier, according to utility FirstEnergy.

Merrin did not respond to requests for comment. In a Facebook post last week, he said Kaptur was "blaming me for a tax break for data centers that was enacted BEFORE I was even elected to the Ohio legislature."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The issue has also featured ​prominently ​in the state's closely watched US Senate race, pitting Republican incumbent Jon Husted against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who lost his old seat in ​2024.

With recent polls showing Brown leading, Republican groups have poured $14 million into advertising in Ohio ‌in the past week alone, hoping to boost Husted's chances.

Brown has repeatedly criticized his opponent for promoting AI infrastructure development and tax incentives, describing him as "data centers' best friend."

"Ohioans, not Jon Husted and his billionaire friends, should get to decide if data centers are built in their community," Brown's campaign said in a statement.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Husted's campaign rejected the criticism, noting he has sponsored legislation that would require data-center operators to cover the cost of building more electricity generation and transmission.

"Sherrod Brown had three decades in Congress to lead on this issue," campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce said in a statement. "Instead, he did nothing and is suddenly pretending to care in the middle of an election year."

TAX SUBSIDY DISCLOSURE GALVANIZES ACTIVISTS

Lyn Cox, a leader of the local advocacy organization Conserve Ohio, said disclosure about the scale of tax subsidies transformed what had been a series of scattered zoning disputes into a statewide political issue.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I think it was a huge turning point," said Cox, who lives in rural Waterville Township, about 40 miles (64 ‌km) from Defiance.

She said candidates from both parties have been forced to engage with activists and develop formal policies on data-center development.

Republican gubernatorial ​candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who previously voiced support for attracting tech investment, released an "Ohioans First" data-center proposal that would eliminate local property-tax abatements for data centers, ​direct revenue toward homeowner rebates and require projects to cover incremental residential electricity costs.

His opponent, Democrat Amy Acton, has ​proposed restricting tax incentives, requiring developers to pay for their own power infrastructure and mandating union labor standards. Both candidates have also called for limiting construction on productive farmland.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Cox remains skeptical of ‌campaign promises from both parties.

"They're just words," she said. "They both came up with a policy ​because they're starting to understand this is a sleeper issue."

Conserve Ohio ​is pursuing a state constitutional amendment in 2027 that would ban the construction of data centers using more than 25 megawatts of power, while supporting similar local ballot initiatives across the state.

Activists are also pressing for more transparency from state officials, who have not disclosed how much revenue local governments have foregone through their own tax agreements with data-center operators.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The companies fueling the AI boom have defended their records.

Amazon says it has invested nearly $40 billion ​in Ohio since 2015; Meta points to more than $2.3 billion worth of investments in the ‌state since 2018. Both companies say their facilities have generated tax revenue, jobs and other economic development.

For residents like Rupp, though, the debate now extends beyond data centers — to whether elected officials are willing to ​defend the public interest against big tech.

"This is definitely a breakdown between what government was supposed to do for small America and what it has failed to do for small America," she said. "I think ​data centers are at the forefront."

(Reporting by Valerie Volcovici in Washington, D.C.; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Timothy Gardner and Rod Nickel)
